plan.analysis: Only evidence is the constant shape at R=2/3. A Gaussian bump already gives about 1/sqrt(2), so the key is nonuniform smooth shapes whose autoconvolution is flatter than a triangle. I will spread across three concrete searches: a generalized-Gaussian family, a direct nonparametric SPSA refinement in log-height space, and a plateau-plus-Gaussian-shoulder family to test whether a flat top in f flattens f*f further. Each returns its best shape at high resolution and uses nearly all of the CPU budget.

experiments.hypothesis: The optimal shape is nonuniform; the generalized Gaussian h(x)=exp(-a|x|^p) with a>0 flattens f*f relative to the constant shape, and Gaussian p=2 already exceeds 2/3.
experiments.change: In construct, ignore start unless it has more than one distinct height. Set x_i=-1+2i/(N-1). Search the two-parameter family h_i=exp(-a|x_i|^p): at least a 30x30 coarse grid plus 500 random points over a in [1e-4,50] log-spaced and p in [0.3,8]. Evaluate exact R using L=[0,*np.convolve(h,h),0] at N=2000 for the search. Then run a local multiplicative pattern search on (a,p), accepting improvements, until 90% of budget_seconds. Return the best (a,p) evaluated at N=20000.
experiments.prediction: The best fit will have a>0 and finite p, with R at least about 0.705 and probably near 0.71. If the best score is <=2/3, this family is the wrong direction.

experiments.hypothesis: A fixed family is too restrictive; direct nonparametric local search in log-height space can refine a good bump and beat any low-dimensional parametric family.
experiments.change: Initialize N=3000 heights as a Gaussian exp(-(x_i/s)^2), choosing s by a 20-point scan over [0.05,1.0] with exact R at N=1000. Optimize z_i=log(h_i) by SPSA: each iteration draw v~N(0,1), evaluate R(h*exp(+delta*v)) and R(h*exp(-delta*v)) with delta=0.01, update z += lr*((R_plus-R_minus)/(2*delta))*v, renormalize mean(h)=1, clip z to [-30,5]. Decay lr and delta on stagnation, smooth z with a tiny Gaussian kernel every 50 iterations, and keep the best h seen. Loop until 0.95*budget_seconds. Return the best h upsampled/interpolated to N=20000.
experiments.prediction: SPSA will improve on the Gaussian seed and reach at least about 0.71-0.72. If it cannot improve over the best simple Gaussian, the local landscape is too rough or the step-size schedule is wrong.

experiments.hypothesis: A flat central plateau with smooth shoulders can make the autoconvolution more rectangular than a Gaussian, raising R above 1/sqrt(2).
experiments.change: Use N=4000, x_i=-1+2i/(N-1), and the family h_i=exp(-a*max(|x_i|-b,0)^p). Search b in [0,0.92], a in [0.05,100] log-spaced, p in [0.5,5] using 500 random triples plus coordinate pattern search, evaluating exact R from L=[0,*np.convolve(h,h),0] at N=2000. Include b=0 as the generalized-Gaussian baseline. Use nearly all of budget_seconds, then return the best triple evaluated at N=20000.
experiments.prediction: The best construction will have b>0 and R above 0.707. If b=0 wins, a plateau in f does not flatten f*f enough to help.

plan.analysis: p0003 is the clear best (0.83786) and its weakness is visible: it optimizes at N=3000 with noisy two-sided SPSA, then merely interpolates to N=20000 without re-optimizing. The target f*f should be as trapezoid-flat as possible; p0003 still has only 36% of knots within 5% of the max and an off-centre peak. I am betting on replacing noisy SPSA with the exact analytic gradient of R at full resolution, plus a coarse-to-fine version to smooth the landscape, and one genuinely different bet: initialize from nonnegative deconvolution of an explicit near-flat trapezoid target before polishing R.

experiments.hypothesis: p0003's SPSA gradient estimate is noisy and its final upsampling is never refined; an exact analytic gradient of R with respect to the 20000 heights should reach a better local optimum and use the full budget efficiently.
experiments.change: Take start, interpolate/trim to N=20000, normalize mean 1, set z=log(h). Implement _R_and_grad(h): L=fftconvolve(h,h); extend by zeros; A=sum(L_i^2+L_iL_{i+1}+L_{i+1}^2)/3; u=dA/dL_i=(L_{i-1}+4L_i+L_{i+1})/3; dA/dh=2*fftconvolve(u,h[::-1])[N-1:2N-1]. Add dB/dh=2*sum(h), and dM/dh from the argmax knot i*: dM[k]=2*h[i*-k] when 0<=i*-k<N. Then dR=(dA*B*M - A*(dB*M+B*dM))/(B*M)^2, and log-gradient g=h*dR. Run Adam on z with lr around 1e-3 to 1e-4, subtract mean(z) each step, clip z to [-30,5], and keep the best R seen. Continue until near the deadline and return the best h at N=20000.
experiments.prediction: Exact-gradient refinement raises the score above 0.845, ideally 0.855-0.87; if it stays below 0.842 then p0003's shape is already near a strong optimum and SPSA noise was not the limiting factor.

experiments.hypothesis: p0003's N=3000 search may sit in a high-resolution local optimum; optimizing the same R by exact gradient on a coarse grid, then repeatedly upsampling and refining, gives a smoother landscape and can find a better basin before high-resolution polishing.
experiments.change: Use the same exact R/gradient routine as experiment 1, but start by block-averaging or interpolating the p0003 start down to N=1000. Run Adam exact-gradient ascent at N=1000, then interpolate the best h to N=2000, refine, then N=4000, 8000, 16000, 20000, spending roughly equal CPU fractions on each stage with the last stage getting extra time. At every stage keep the best-R array; at the final resolution run until the deadline and return the best N=20000 array. Do not reset the step size to a large value between stages; halve it when upsampling.
experiments.prediction: Coarse-to-fine exact gradient matches or beats the full-resolution run; a score above 0.85 indicates the low-resolution search was the bottleneck, while a score below experiment 1 suggests global coarse search does not help and local full-resolution refinement is sufficient.

experiments.hypothesis: Directly optimizing R from p0003 may be trapped in one basin; fitting f to an explicitly near-trapezoidal target f*f, whose ideal R is close to 1, can produce a different nonnegative shape that is a better starting point for R refinement.
experiments.change: Build discrete target g_w of length 2N-1 on [0,2]: plateau height 1 from x=w to 2-w, linear cosine/linear tapers of width w at both ends, for w in {0.08, 0.15}. Initialize z=log(h) from the p0003 start. For a short phase (about 20-30% of budget), minimize J(z)=||conv(exp(z),exp(z))-c*g_w||^2 using the same convolution-gradient machinery but differentiating J rather than R (normalize g_w or choose c to match total mass). Do this for both w, keep the candidate with the highest actual R. Then spend the remaining budget running the exact R-gradient Adam ascent from that best candidate, while also keeping p0003 itself as a fallback if its R is higher. Return the best N=20000 array found.
experiments.prediction: The deconvolution start initially scores below p0003, but after R ascent either it enters a new basin and exceeds 0.845-0.86, or it falls back to p0003; a final score below 0.84 would refute near-flat target fitting as a useful initialization for this problem.

plan.analysis: p0009 is the clear best line: analytic gradients in log-height space improved p0003 by +0.026. But its code spends the whole budget in the N=8000 loop, so the intended N=20000 polish never runs; FFT convolution can make full-resolution iterations cheap. p0009 also uses a nonsmooth single-argmax L-infinity gradient, and resolution beyond 20k is untested. I bet one experiment on actually using the full 20k polish, one on smoothing the max to flatten the near-max plateau, and one on coarse-to-fine continuation to 100k steps.

experiments.hypothesis: p0009 never executes its N=20000 polish because the N=8000 main loop consumes the deadline; FFT convolution makes full-resolution Adam fast enough to use both stages.
experiments.change: In p0009, import scipy.signal and replace np.convolve in _R_from_h and _R_and_grad by fftconvolve(..., mode='full') truncated to length 2*n-1. Set deadline_main = t0 + 0.75*budget. Run the existing N=8000 Adam loop only until deadline_main. Then interpolate best_h to Nout=20000, reset Adam moments, and run a full Adam/log-height loop at Nout until t0+0.95*budget, tracking best_out by exact _R_from_h. Return best_out.
experiments.prediction: Score rises above 0.863731, likely to 0.866-0.870; more importantly the N=20000 stage will actually consume CPU time near the deadline.

experiments.hypothesis: The exact max in R is nonsmooth and sends gradient only through one argmax knot, which may prevent the many near-max knots of f*f from flattening into a better plateau.
experiments.change: In _R_and_grad, keep the exact max m_exact for tracking, but use a smoothed denominator m_s = tau*logsumexp(L/tau) for the gradient. Compute w = softmax(L/tau) and dmdh = 2*convolve(w, h[::-1])[n-1:2*n-1]. Use R_smooth = N/(s^2*m_s) in the gradient formula, with tau annealed as tau = max(0.002*m_exact, 0.1*m_exact*0.995**(step//20)). Track best_h using exact _R_from_h. Keep all other p0009 Adam settings and N=8000.
experiments.prediction: Score exceeds 0.863731 by at least 0.001-0.003 if the max plateau is not already locally flat; a flat result would show the exact-max gradient is sufficient.

experiments.hypothesis: p0009 stops at N=20000 after interpolating from N=8000; optimizing at increasing resolutions with FFT should better approximate the continuous optimal shape and exploit finer structure.
experiments.change: Use fftconvolve for L and for dNdh in all R/gradient calls. Run three Adam/log-height stages: N=10000 until t0+0.35*budget, N=40000 until t0+0.65*budget, and N=100000 until t0+0.95*budget. At each stage interpolate the previous best_h to the new N, reset Adam moments, use lr 0.04, 0.025, 0.015 respectively, and scale smoothing sigma to 0.7*N/10000. Track best at each resolution using exact _R_from_h and return the best N=100000 array.
experiments.prediction: Score exceeds 0.863731, likely reaching 0.866-0.870; if it does not, resolution above 20k is not a limiting factor.
